headline: Approved prior meeting minutes; discussed Salem Common tree planting plan, permit outreach, and spotted lanternfly.
summary: Members heard reports on tree work, storm hazards, and planting from the Tree Warden and a DCR forester. They discussed a 12-year plan for trees on Salem Common and the spotted lanternfly. The only vote was to approve the June minutes, with one member abstaining.
decisions: Approved the Tree Commission minutes of June 8, 2026, by roll call vote, with one member abstaining.

decision_evidence.quote: Mr. Rieder moved to approve the Tree Commission Meeting Minutes for June 8, 2026. Seconded by Ms. McCarter. A roll call vote was taken, and the motion was carried. Jessica Choi abstained.

MINUTES OF THE SALEM TREE COMMISSION 
MONDAY, SEPTEMBER 14, 2026 
 
A meeting of the Salem Tree Commission was held on September 14, 2026, at 7:00 p.m., via 
ZOOM, an online video conference call system in accordance with Chapter 2 of the Acts of 
2025. 
1. Present were Chair Darleen Melis; Vice Chair Kirt Rieder ; M embers: Jessica Choi, Paul 
L’Heureux, Rachel McCarter, Jacob St. Louis and Susan Yochelson; Tree Warden Kieran 
Kavanaugh and Commission  Clerk Joanne Roomey. Absent w ere Cady Goldfield and David 
Livingston. 
2. Report – Kieran Kavanaugh, Tree Warden (watering new trees, tree removal at Loring 
Ave., Mack Park treatments by Park Dept.) 
Kieran reported that there have been 19 emergency calls since the start of the fiscal year, with 
recent microbursts resulting in downed limbs and other storm -related hazards. Residents are 
encouraged to report dangerous or cracked limbs as soon as possible. He also informed us that 
his department is responsible for removing wasp nests so please report any that you see. He 
also observed that at this time of year many people are posting signs on trees , which is a 
violation. He encouraged that we report such infractions to him rather than removing them so 
that staff can document and address the violations. 
Since the start of the fiscal year, the department has completed 63 plantings, with 14 additional 
trees recently delivered  and approximately 35 more plantings anticipated for the fall. The 
Department now has three full-time employees, significantly increasing its capacity for work 
orders, plantings, removals, and remediation. However, the foreman has taken some personal 
time off an d the tw o new employees need more training before they can work  without 
supervision.  
Updating conditions at Palmer Cove – he reported that the department completed remediation 
work, including removing old plantings and dead trees, trimming dead wood, and planting  
seven new trees. Regarding the Riverwalk / Juniper Drive project, the department reported that 
a demand notice has been issued to Mr. Tranos, with an update to follow once the matter is 
finalized. 
Darleen asked about who removed trees at the intersection of Crombie and Norman Street s. 
Kieran explained that the department was contacted and after inspection he approved removal 
because the trees presented  an imminent hazard. The trees were replaced with shrubs  by the

business however, Darleen observed that this was inappropriate since they were larger than 8-
inch DBH Protected Trees and the expectation is that they should be replaced with trees. Kieran 
offered that they since they were not an elective removal and since there is not much space at 
that location, he will have a conversation about planting and the DBH loss.  
3. Greening the Gateway Cities Program – David Bresnahan, DCR Forester  
 
Dave provided an update on the tree planting program. He said that its crew has planted 
more than 1,700 trees in Salem since 2021, not including the grant funded plantings. 
Statewide the Greening the Gateway Cities Program has planted nearly 60,000 trees. The 
Salem crew includes two laborers and a forestry assistant and is currently in its second week 
of fall planting primarily on private residential and business properties. Property owners, 
tenants, or business owners are responsible for watering and aftercare. 
DCR is planting a mix of tree stock and is considering planting some bare-root stock later in 
the fall. The program has discontinued planting cherry and dogwood cornus species due to 
poor establishment and disease concerns. Staff are also limiting fall planting of certain 
species, including tupelo, redbud, and sweetgum in fall plantings , based on survivorship 
research. Five locations have been identified for planting in the Point neighborhood, including 
some empty tree pits, and the housing authority property at the corner of Leavitt and Congress 
Streets where dogwoods did not survive. He welcomes suggestions for species to be planted 
at these locations. He also mentioned that  3 ft cages placed around newly planted trees is 
helping to protect the roots and helping to keep them alive. 
Dave also said that Salem Sound Coastwatch received a partnership grant to support outreach 
for the current fiscal year. DCR plans to connect with the organization’s new leadership and 
explore outreach opportunities, including tabling at the Salem Farmers’ Market. 
At Salem State University, approximately 90 trees planted by DCR are growing well. The 
University is making some  progress removing volcano- style mulch berms around newly 
planted and established trees, and they have  taken on the responsibility for watering and 
maintaining the trees.  
Darleen observed that newly planted  willows at Salem Willows Park have been overly 
mulched. Kieran said that this is the city’s responsibility and he will investigate it. 
4. Tree Permit Visibility on City Website  
 
The Commission discussed ways to increase visibility and compliance with tree permit 
requirements. While larger tree removal companies are familiar with the city’s permitting 
process, smaller and out-of-town landscaping companies may not be aware of the 
requirements. Kieran is working with IT and other departments to streamline the online and 
paper permitting systems into one automated process and identify opportunities to prompt 
applicants when a tree permit may be required. Kieran wants to continue the social media 
initiative, reaching out to other entities to help us get our messages across. Jessica Choi 
volunteered to help reaching out to different outlets.
3 
The Commission also discussed outreach to local landscaping companies and increasing 
public awareness through Tree City USA signage, potentially including a “Tree Permits 
Required” message. 
5. Tree Steward event – Saturday, Sept. 12 on Chestnut St. 
Darleen said the Tree Steward event was very successful, with several residents from the 
neighborhood, even those who are knowledgeable about other forms of horticulture showing 
strong interest in tree care. Volunteers worked on trees in front of  28 Chestnut Street, 
removing built-up soil and grass from around the trees to expose the proper root level. The 
work also provided an opportunity to demonstrate a new technique using a hose to flush out 
soil, which proved effective  in this setting. The event was a valuable learning experience, 
and the neighbors were very engaged in caring for the trees. One of the city’s last remaining 
elm trees was also highlighted. 
6. Future Tree Plantings on Salem Common 
Kieran reported that the city is finalizing a contract with a landscape architect for a 12-year 
planting plan for the existing trees on Salem Common. The project will focus on the health 
and management of existing trees and will not include new plantings that encroach on the 
green space. The plan will be phased over Years 1, 4, 8, and 12 and will include a current 
health assessment of all trees within the Common , a level 2 tree risk assessment,  and an 
inventory and tagging of existing trees. Funding options are being finalized, with the 
landscape architect expected to begin work soon. 
Darleen noted that the city was awarded $50,000 through State Senator Joan Lovely, with 
approximately $30,000 designated for planting. The Salem Tree Donation Fund also has 
approximately $30,000 available for planting, while the Salem Common Receipts Reserve  
Fund has over $60,500. Darleen suggested using the reserve funds to hire the arborist first, 
as the landscape architect will need the arborist’s findings to develop the planting plan. 
Darleen also emphasized that the Salem Common Neighborhood Association, Friends of 
Salem Common, Parks Department, Trish O’Brien, and the Tree Warden should be involved 
as key stakeholders throughout the project. Kieran noted that he is hoping to continue the 
planting with Lahey Landscaping whose contract is up this calendar year. 
Darleen asked Kieran to connect with T odd Dunlop, the Grounds Director Salem Hospital 
about a large tree between their property an d Bertram Field that is overhanging the 
concession stand. She also reported that all of the trees on Rte. 107 by the hospital are dead. 
Kirt Reider said he would talk to the Planning Board about red maples below the track that 
on the ER access road have died, that should be replaced because there was an obligation to 
keep them alive. 
7.  Approve Tree Commission Minutes of June 8, 2026 
Mr. Rieder moved to approve the Tree  Commission Meeting Minutes for June 8, 2026. 
Seconded by Ms. McCarter. A roll call vote was taken, and the motion was carried. Jessica 
Choi abstained.
4 
8. New Business 
Members discussed concerns raised by a recent Boston Globe article regarding the spotted 
lanternfly and its potential impact on city trees. It was noted that lanternflies primarily favor 
Tree of Heaven but can spread to other tree species, including maples. Members discussed 
reports that populations of these insects may decline after several years . The impact of 
lanternflies on existing trees and consideration of the pest in future plantings was raised. 
Kirt asked about updates on public trees near the Life Bridge project on Margin Street. 
9. Questions from the audience - None 
10. Next Meeting Dates: Monday, October 19, 2026 at 7:00 p.m. and November 16, 2026 
via Zoom. 
11. Adjournment: There being  no further business to come before the Tree Commission this 
evening, Mr. L’Heureux moved to adjourn. Seconded by Mr. St. Louis . A roll call vote was 
taken, and the motion was carried unanimously. The meeting was adjourned at 8:10 p.m. 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
 
Joanne M. Roomey 
Commission Clerk
